Q: How can I generate a .bin executable file with MPLAB X IDE? A:

After hours of reaserch on the web, I found the way:

In MPLAB project properties window select "Building" and the tell the compiler to execute this macro after building:

${MP_CC_DIR}\xc16-objcopy -I ihex -O binary "${DISTDIR}/${PROJECTNAME}.${IMAGE_TYPE}.hex" "${DISTDIR}/${PROJECTNAME}.${IMAGE_TYPE}.bin"

The image shows how to do it:

That's it.

Now the issue is understand why the generated bin file is near 10 times bigger than the .hex file, but I will make another specific post for that, because I have not the slightest idea...

Q: How do I get file file contents for the entire project from a different branch? A:

Use git worktree add /path/to/foo temp to checkout foo under /path/to/foo. main is still unchanged under the current repository.

If the changes on main are not committed yet,

# option 1
# on main
# create a stash entry
git stash
# apply it without removing it from the stash list
git stash apply

cd /path/to/foo
# on temp
git stash apply
git add .
git commit

# option 2
# on main
git diff > /path/to/patch.diff

cd /path/to/foo
# on temp
git apply -3 /path/to/patch.diff
git add .
git commit

If the changes have been committed in commit1,

cd /path/to/foo
# on temp
git cherry-pick $commit1

After the changes are committed on temp, you can remove the worktree.

cd /path/to/main
git worktree remove -f /path/to/foo

# or
rm -rf /path/to/foo
git worktree prune

Q: Is there a reason to have both tox.ini and setup.cfg in a python project? A:

PyScaffold is a tool which tries to ease the setup of a new Python project.

At the very heart a single executable Python file is enough.

If you want to make the project being installable, you need configuration file for the build system.

While a lot has changed, still setup.py is the most prominent one. It may not be a great idea that the build configuration file could execute arbitrary code, so setup.cfg was invented, where you can define e.g. the projects name and dependencies in a ini-style format. Meanwhile, another format was invented, the pyproject.toml file.

So basically, to build your project you need one of those:

  • setup.py
  • setup.py and setup.cfg (the former only calls the latter)
  • pyproject.toml

Usually you want to write tests. You could use the builtin unittest testrunner to run your tests, or nowadays many projects use pytest. pytest can be configured with a pytest.ini.

Tests usually need some dependencies, e.g. pytest itself and maybe some other test helpers. They need to be installed at some time.

And here comes tox into play. Amongst many other features, like e.g. running your tests against different Python versions, tox can both install your project and your test requirements and execute the tests. tox usually comes with a tox.ini file.

What about linting? You want to have easy to read code and follow Python guidelines (e.g. PEP 8), so you usually use a tool like flake8 - which also comes with its own configuration file, namely .flake8.

We have many tools and many configuration files, but that's not all. As not everybody likes so many configuration files, some of the tools support to be configured with other tools's configuration file.

e.g. you can configure flake8 both in a setup.cfg and a tox.ini, see https://flake8.pycqa.org/en/latest/user/configuration.html

You can also configure tox via setup.cfg or pyproject.toml, see https://tox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/config.html#configuration-discovery

You only need to configure your tool once, not in all those files.

So, technically, you do not need all those files, and it is up to you what you think is an easy to read and easy to manage setup for your project.

I gave a 5 minute talk about how this is all confusing and my solution:

https://youtu.be/8iqhNbDHC-c

Q: Google Sheets - Function to cross data - issue on data range A:

you can use REDUCE for this purpose:

=REDUCE(TOCOL(,1), A1:A10, LAMBDA(x, y, VSTACK(x, INDIRECT(y))))

where A1:A10 are your sheet names with a range eg. A1 for example would read Sheet2!A2:C3

Q: DAX: Why does COUNTROWS with a FILTER defining the table return an error? A:

When writing this in Dax Studio, the result from countrows needs to be accessed through a statement; solution found here: https://community.powerbi.com/t5/DAX-Commands-and-Tips/The-expression-specified-in-the-query-is-not-a-valid-table/m-p/889744#M7817

DEFINE
test_measure = 
  COUNTROWS(
    FILTER(
      'galaxies',
      'galaxies'[name] = "Milky Way"
      )
  )

EVALUATE
ROW("Result",test_measure)
